A field guide / Definitions

Internal, cloud, and background agents, explained

Three simple questions help make sense of these labels: What work is it for? Where does it run? How do you interact with it?

An agent can be internal, cloud, and background at the same time. Each word tells you something different about it.

This guide offers practical definitions for understanding and describing agents.

The three terms ↓Examples on the map ↓Common questions ↓

01 / Three independent properties

Three terms, three questions

01

What work is it for?

Internal agent

An agent used within an organization to carry out its own workflows, with access to the company context, tools, and permissions it needs.

02

Where does it run?

Cloud agent

An agent whose execution environment runs on cloud infrastructure, independently of the user's device.

03

How do you interact with it?

Background agent

An agent working without continuous user interaction, able to request input or approval when needed.

Internal: built around the organization's work

An internal agent might help employees resolve IT issues, investigate a failed deployment, or process invoices. Its job is part of the organization's own operations.

The company can build it from scratch or configure an existing product. “Internal” describes the work it serves; it doesn't require the company to build the underlying model or host the software itself.

Cloud: running independently of your device

A cloud agent runs its work on hosted infrastructure. Depending on how the service is designed, you might start a task on your laptop and check the result from your phone.

The label describes where execution happens. Whether the agent stays running, pauses, or resumes later depends on the system behind it.

Background: working without continuous attention

A background agent can begin with a direct request, a schedule, or an event such as a new support ticket. You don't need to supervise every step.

When you actively work with it, the interaction moves into the foreground. The agent can move between these modes as the task requires.

02 / Labels can overlap

One agent can be all three

Imagine an invoice agent for a finance team. It checks new invoices against purchase orders on a cloud computer and asks an employee to approve payments.

If an employee opens a conversation to resolve a mismatch, the interaction moves into the foreground. The agent still serves the same team and runs in the same place.

03 / Authority is another question

What can it do without approval?

Autonomy describes the decisions and actions an agent can take without human approval.

The invoice agent might match records automatically but require approval before issuing a payment. It works in the background with limited authority.

Be specific when describing that authority:

“It can match invoices automatically. Payments require approval.”
Match invoicesAgent can act→Approve paymentHuman decision→Issue paymentAfter approval

Working without your attention is different from acting without your permission.

05 / Common questions

Frequently asked questions

Are internal, cloud, and background agents competing categories?

They describe different aspects of an agent, so the labels can overlap. An internal agent can run locally or in the cloud and work in the foreground or background.

What is a foreground agent?

An agent operating through active interaction with a user. For example, you might discuss a problem, review its findings, and give it further instructions as it works. Foreground and background describe modes the same agent can move between.

What is a local agent?

An agent whose execution environment runs on your device. It may still send requests to a model hosted in the cloud. For this guide, local and cloud describe where the agent's work runs; the model can be hosted separately.

Does an internal agent have to be built in-house?

No. A company can configure an existing agent around an internal workflow. The relevant distinction is the work it performs and the company context and access it uses.

Does internal mean private or self-hosted?

The label alone tells you neither. An internal agent can use hosted services. Data handling, access controls, and hosting arrangements are separate properties to check.

Does a background agent need a schedule?

A schedule is one option. A person can ask it to work on a task and return later, or an event can trigger it. Background describes the level of ongoing interaction, not what starts the work.

Does a cloud agent keep working when I close my laptop?

It can, if the service supports independent execution. Cloud hosting makes execution independent of your device, but continued work also depends on session rules, time limits, and how tasks are managed.

Is every agent used by a company an internal agent?

For this guide, internal means serving the organization's own operations. An agent answering customers directly is better described as customer-facing. A system can serve both audiences, so describe the particular role you're discussing.

Are these official definitions?

These are working definitions for clearer communication. Product names may use the terms differently. Asking about purpose, execution, interaction, and authority helps you understand what a particular agent actually does.
